q-350330.name: Question 1
q-350330.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{3}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{x}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{-3/2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{a}^{3}}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{3}}}) \\  & =-2(0-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-152045.name: Question 3
q-152045.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=2x+4.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x+4$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $4$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{(2x+4)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}(\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{(2x+4)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{4}^{\infty }{u}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{4}^{a}{u}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-2{u}^{-1/2}]}_{4}^{a} \\  & =-3\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}]}_{4}^{a} \\  & =-3\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}] \\  & =-3\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-152053.name: Question 4
q-152053.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=1+{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=1+{x}^{3}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{{(1+{x}^{3})}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{{(1+{x}^{3})}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}{u}^{-3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{a}^{3}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-100634.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2-3z}\,\text{d}z & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{2-3z}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|2-3z|]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-3z|]_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-3a|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|-1|) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-3a|) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\infty ) \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

q-100643.name: Question 8
q-100643.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{\text{d}t}{\sqrt{2-3t}} & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{\text{d}t}{\sqrt{2-3t}} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{2-3t}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\sqrt{2+3}-\sqrt{2-3a}) \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}+\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\sqrt{2-3a} \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}+\infty  \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

q-100642.name: Question 9
q-100642.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2z+1}}\,\text{d}z & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2z+1}}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{3}{2}(2z+1)^{2/3}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[(2z+1)^{2/3}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }((2a+1)^{2/3}-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \infty  \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

q-80342.name: Question 10
q-80342.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{\text{d}z}{\sqrt{1-z}} & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{\text{d}z}{\sqrt{1-z}} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-2\sqrt{1-z}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\sqrt{1-0}-\sqrt{1-a}) \\  & =-2+2\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }\sqrt{1-a} \\  & =-2+2\cdot \infty  \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.
